**Disclosure:** A4 already read this test set to compare the classifier with the LLM, so these numbers are not fully untouched. Nothing below was tuned on it: the threshold and the fraud rule are chosen on validation only.

## 2. Error costs (units: one misrouted ticket)

| error | who pays | cost |
|---|---|---|
| false negative on `fraud_security` (fraud routed as routine) | the customer waits while money may be leaving | R (2, 5, 10 or 20; A4 used 5) |
| false positive on `fraud_security` (routine escalated as fraud) | the fraud team spends time | 2.0 |
| any other confusion | ticket in the wrong queue, re-triaged | 1.0 |
| deferral to the LLM | one call plus latency, and the LLM can be wrong too | 0.3 + the LLM's own error cost |

## 3. The A4 gap: how good is the LLM on the tickets the classifier defers?

Measured on the **validation** tickets below A4's threshold (0.7): 118 tickets (0 LLM calls failed and are excluded from the LLM figure).

| | accuracy on the deferred tickets |
|---|---|
| classifier's own answer | 0.627 |
| LLM (`LLM_PROMPT`, temperature 0) | 0.644 |

Difference (LLM minus classifier): +0.017, 95% bootstrap interval -0.102 to +0.127 on 118 paired tickets. 15 of them are true `fraud_security`.

**The LLM is not shown to be better than the classifier on these tickets** (the interval includes zero), and it is far from the 'always right' assumption A4 used. Sending low-confidence tickets to the LLM buys no measurable accuracy; a human-review queue is the better destination (recommended, not built: out of scope).

### Per-class view: a lower alert level for fraud

Rule: also defer when P(`fraud_security`) is at least the alert level although another class won, so a likely fraud ticket is never silently routed as routine.
